name: อาการปวดท้องบรรเทาได้ด้วยอาการท้องอืด
pinyin: fù tòng dé shǐ qì zé shū
preview_text: อาการปวดท้องที่บรรเทาลงหลังจากขับแก๊สไม่ได้เป็นเพียง 'IBS' เท่านั้น แต่ยังเป็นสัญญาณว่าพลังชี่ของตับหรือลำไส้เล็กของคุณติดอยู่ คนส่วนใหญ่สังเกตเห็นอาการท้องอืดน้อยลงและอาการปวดน้อยลง ...
synonyms: ["Belly Pain Relieved By Flatulence", "Gas-relieved Abdominal Pain", "Stomach Pain Eased By Passing Gas", "Passing gas that temporarily relieves discomfort", "Pain relieved by passing gas", "Passing gas brings temporary relief", "Passing gas provides temporary relief", "Relief after passing gas"]
conventional_description: In conventional medicine, abdominal pain that improves with passing gas is often attributed to functional gastrointestinal disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), dyspepsia, or excessive intestinal gas. The pain is thought to result from heightened sensitivity to normal gut distension or altered motility, where trapped gas stretches the bowel wall. Diagnosis typically involves ruling out structural causes through history, exam, and sometimes imaging or endoscopy.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on symptom relief: over-the-counter simethicone to break up gas bubbles, antispasmodics for cramping, and dietary changes like a low-FODMAP diet to reduce gas production. Stress reduction and probiotics may also be recommended. For persistent symptoms, prescription medications targeting gut motility or visceral hypersensitivity are sometimes used.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, pain that gets better after passing gas or belching is a hallmark of Qi stagnation - a state where the body’s Qi is stuck and not flowing smoothly. The abdomen is particularly sensitive to this because the Stomach and Intestines are designed to move contents downward. When emotional stress or dietary factors disrupt this downward movement, Qi backs up, causing distension and cramping.
The Liver plays a central role. It is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and when it becomes stagnant - often from frustration or unexpressed anger - it can ‘invade’ the Stomach. This causes upper abdominal pain that radiates to the ribs, belching, and relief from both belching and flatulence. This pattern is very common in people whose pain worsens with stress.
If the stagnation settles lower in the abdomen, the Small Intestine may be the main organ involved. Here, trapped Qi creates a twisting, wandering pain around the navel, often with loud gurgling sounds. The pain may feel cold and improves with warmth and passing gas. This pattern, called Small Intestine Qi Pain, can also be triggered by emotional tension but often has a colder quality.
Because the same Western diagnosis of ‘functional abdominal pain’ can stem from different TCM patterns, treatment must be tailored. The location of the pain, what makes it better or worse, and the emotional state at onset are all clues that guide a practitioner to the right pattern - and the right herbs and acupuncture points.
classical_translation: "Abdominal pain that is relieved by passing gas is due to Qi stagnation."
classical_source:
Yi Zong Jin Jian (Golden Mirror of Medicine)  ,  Volume on Abdominal Pain 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first listens to the story of the pain: where it sits, how it feels, and what makes it better or worse. Abdominal pain that eases after passing gas or belching immediately points toward Qi stagnation - the discomfort comes from trapped movement, and releasing the gas temporarily frees the flow. The next step is to figure out which organ system is most involved.
When the pain is mainly in the upper belly and rib area, comes in waves of cramping and distension, and flares up during times of stress or frustration, the pattern is usually Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. The tongue often has a thin white coating, and the pulse feels wiry, like a guitar string. The emotional trigger is the big clue here, because the Liver’s Qi becomes stuck when feelings are held in, and then it lashes sideways into the Stomach.
If the pain is lower down, around the navel or below, and seems to move from place to place with loud gurgling sounds, a practitioner considers Small Intestine Qi Pain. This pattern can still be stirred by emotional tension, but it often has a colder quality - the abdomen may feel better with warmth, and the tongue might look pale with a white coat. The pulse is still wiry, but may also feel tight, reflecting a mix of Qi stagnation and Cold.
To confirm, the practitioner will gently palpate the abdomen and ask about bowel habits, appetite, and sleep. A history of irritable moods and belching points upward toward the Liver-Stomach picture, while lower abdominal cramping with rumbling and a preference for warmth guides the diagnosis toward the Small Intestine. The difference in location and temperature sensation is often the deciding factor.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending, cramping pain in the upper abdomen that radiates to the ribs", "Pain worsens with emotional stress or frustration", "Frequent belching or acid reflux", "Irritability and easy anger", "Feeling of stuffiness in the chest and frequent sighing", "Pain is relieved by passing gas or belching"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress or anger, Frustration or resentment, Irregular eating or skipping meals, Greasy or heavy foods, Alcohol or caffeine
patterns.better_with: Passing gas or belching, Warm compress on the abdomen, Gentle movement or stretching, Relaxation and stress reduction, Small, regular meals
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When emotional stress or frustration causes the Liver Qi to stagnate, it often invades the Stomach, disrupting its downward-moving Qi. This results in a trapped, distending pain in the upper abdomen that radiates to the ribcage. Passing gas or belching temporarily releases the pent-up Qi, bringing immediate relief.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body, may have redder sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦, xián), most pronounced at the left middle (Liver) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly causes Liver Qi to stagnate and rise, invading the Stomach and creating the distending pain. Passing gas or belching releases the trapped Qi, providing immediate relief. Warmth and gentle movement help to unblock Qi flow, while heavy, greasy foods and irregular eating further stagnate Qi in the middle burner, worsening symptoms.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, smaller meals and avoid greasy, fried, or spicy foods that burden the Stomach. Incorporate gentle daily exercise like walking or yoga to keep Qi moving. Practice stress management such as meditation or deep breathing. Avoid eating when upset.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Small Intestine receives and separates food, and its Qi can easily become knotted when emotional stress or Cold disrupts the Liver’s ability to keep things flowing. This stagnation settles in the lower abdomen, causing Qi to twist and cramp. The pain moves around, and loud gurgling sounds arise as the trapped Qi struggles to move. Passing gas provides a brief release, which is why the pain temporarily eases.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a thin white coat. Pulse: deep (Chen) and wiry (Xian), possibly tight if Cold is present.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which directly disrupts the Small Intestine’s Qi flow, leading to pain. Cold contracts and obstructs Qi, worsening the stagnation. Warmth and gentle movement help unblock Qi, while passing gas releases the trapped Qi, temporarily relieving pressure. Therefore, managing stress and keeping the abdomen warm are key.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals and avoid raw, cold foods that can constrict Qi. Gentle daily movement like walking helps keep Qi flowing. Manage stress with relaxation techniques, as emotional tension directly tightens the abdomen. A warm compress on the lower belly can provide comfort.

faqs.question: Why does my stomach pain go away after I pass gas?
faqs.answer: In TCM, this is a clear sign that your pain is caused by Qi stagnation - trapped energy that needs to move. Passing gas temporarily releases that pressure, allowing Qi to flow again. The relief is like opening a valve. However, if the underlying stagnation isn't addressed, the gas and pain will build up again. Treatment focuses on keeping Qi moving smoothly so you don't have to rely on passing gas for relief.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help with gas and bloating?
faqs.answer: Yes. TCM excels at treating functional digestive issues like gas, bloating, and cramping because it directly targets the flow of Qi. Acupuncture and herbs help regulate the movement of the Stomach and Intestines, reducing the buildup of trapped gas. Many patients find that after a few weeks of treatment, they feel less bloated and have more comfortable digestion overall.

faqs.question: Is this just IBS?
faqs.answer: It could be, but TCM looks beyond the label. While IBS is a common Western diagnosis for this kind of pain, TCM identifies specific patterns - like Liver invading Stomach or Small Intestine Qi Pain - that explain why your symptoms behave the way they do. The pattern determines the treatment, so even two people with the same IBS diagnosis might receive different herbs and acupuncture points.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: Most people notice some improvement within 2-4 weeks, especially if the pattern is Liver Qi Stagnation. Pain episodes often become less intense and shorter. For deeper or colder patterns, it may take 4-6 weeks. Consistency with herbs and weekly acupuncture is important - missing treatments can slow progress. Long-standing issues may need a few months to fully resolve.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. You don't need an extreme overhaul, but simple shifts - like eating warm, cooked foods and avoiding cold, raw meals - can make a big difference. Greasy and fried foods tend to worsen stagnation. Your practitioner may offer specific advice based on your pattern, but the baseline is to eat calmly and regularly, with an emphasis on easy-to-digest foods.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with trapped gas?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can stimulate the movement of Qi in the digestive tract, often providing immediate relief from trapped gas and bloating. Points like Tianshu ST-25 and Zusanli ST-36 are commonly used to regulate intestinal function. While a single session may help, regular treatments build a more lasting effect by retraining the body's Qi flow.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take herbs with my current medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but always tell your TCM practitioner about all medications you take. Some Qi-moving herbs can interact with blood thinners or sedatives. Your practitioner will adjust the formula to avoid interactions. Never stop a prescribed medication without consulting your doctor. If you have any concerns, bring your medication list to your first appointment.

research.title: Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome
research.description: This Cochrane systematic review assessed acupuncture for IBS and found that acupuncture significantly improved abdominal pain and overall symptoms compared to sham acupuncture and pharmacological therapies, with a favourable safety profile.
research.periodical: Manheimer E, Wieland LS, Cheng K, et al. Acupuncture for irritable bowel syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012;(5):CD005111.

research.title: Chaihu Shugan San for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found that Chaihu Shugan San, alone or combined with conventional treatment, significantly relieved epigastric pain, postprandial fullness, and belching in patients with functional dyspepsia, supporting its use for Qi stagnation patterns.
research.periodical: Xiao Y, Liu Y, Yu K, et al. Chaihu Shugan San for functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2019;238:111841.
